claim: The CRA covers products with digital elements with a direct or indirect data connection, regulates design/development/production and vulnerability handling, and can apply alongside the Machinery Regulation.

CRA vulnerability and incident reporting applies from 11 September 2026, with 24-hour early warning, 72-hour notification and a vulnerability final report within 14 days after a corrective or mitigating measure is available; main obligations apply from 11 December 2027.
ENISA says the Single Reporting Platform will be used by manufacturers and CSIRTs for mandatory CRA reporting from 11 September 2026.

Manufacturers must document cybersecurity aspects and vulnerabilities, update risk assessments where appropriate, operate vulnerability disclosure, handle vulnerabilities through a support period normally at least five years, and keep technical documentation updated where appropriate during that period; industrial products are often used longer.

claim: The Data Act definition of connected product covers products collecting use or environmental data, able to communicate product data, and not primarily storing or transmitting data for another party.
The European Commission gives robots and industrial machines as examples of connected products under the Data Act.
source_locator: excerpts/01-data-examples.txt — Chapter II, “Examples of connected products”

claim: Data Act Article 3 requires accessible product/related-service data and metadata by design plus pre-contract information; Article 4 requires readily available data on simple electronic request where feasible when it is not directly accessible.
The Data Act applies generally from 12 September 2025; Article 3(1) applies to connected products and related services placed on the market after 12 September 2026.
The Data Act requires measures and written substantiation around withholding or suspending access to trade-secret data and notification of the competent authority in defined cases.

A 2024 qualitative survey covered seven large industrial-equipment manufacturers and five consultancies/partners, mostly Northern European and recruited partly through a compliance-automation research project; all manufacturer participants already had an IEC 62443-4-1-aligned SDL.

Survey participants described organisational ownership, SDL enforcement, update management, expertise, vulnerability management and the notification deadline as challenges, with organisational/procedural issues often harder than technical controls.
In the twelve-organisation survey, 50% expected cost impacts below 20%, 25% no cost impact and 50% no role changes; the authors say existing-resource compliance is one possible explanation.
